meta_home_title: EpiDetective — Open tools for reading health evidence
meta_home_desc: Free tools that let you explore the published evidence on what causes cancer and other major chronic diseases. Built by a cancer epidemiologist at IARC/WHO.
meta_explorer_desc: See which exposures have been linked to which cancers, and how strong the evidence is for each link. Built on the WHO's IARC Monographs.
home_h1: Translating epidemiological evidence for a healthier world
home_audience: For the curious public, patients, doctors, journalists, and the people who write health policy.
home_lede: EpiDetective builds free tools that let you explore published health research for yourself.
inst_h2: Two are open now. More are being built.
inst_t1_desc: See which exposures have been linked to which cancers, and how strong the evidence is behind each link. It is built on the IARC Monographs, the World Health Organization's review of what can cause cancer. Start from a cancer, start from an exposure, or open the whole map.
inst_t2_desc: Which risk factors have been linked to heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, dementia, cancer and other major chronic conditions — and how strong the evidence is behind each link, including where it is genuinely contested. Pull the network apart to see how the risk factors group together.
about_h2: Built by a cancer epidemiologist who works with this data every day.
about_p1: I am Wenxin Wan, a postdoctoral researcher at the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), the World Health Organization's cancer agency, based in Lyon, France.
about_p2: I earned my PhD at Utrecht University's Institute for Risk Assessment Sciences in the Netherlands, studying how exposures at work and in the environment shape cancer risk at the population level. Part of that work provided new evidence on the causal relationship between benzene and lung cancer, and was covered by The New York Times.
about_p3: My daily work at IARC revolves around large international cohorts: millions of people followed over many years so that the risk factors causally linked to disease can be identified. I lead the analysis and coordinate the project for OPICO, the international opioid cohort consortium, which brings ten cohorts from three continents together to ask what cancer risk long-term opioid use may carry; and I serve as scientific advisor to the Lung Cancer Cohort Consortium (LC3), helping carry the evidence built up by occupational-exposure research into lung cancer screening for populations worldwide.
about_p4: I have spent years helping to produce this kind of evidence myself, yet far too little of it ever reaches ordinary people — the very people the research was meant to protect. That has frustrated me for a long time. A finding that stays inside the literature has done less than half its job. Closing that distance is worth every bit of effort we can give it, and that is why I created this site.

It carries no endorsement from the International Agency for Research on Cancer or the World Health Organization, and the views expressed here belong to the author alone. The underlying scientific sources are cited so that anyone can check them independently.
foot_disclaimer: EpiDetective publishes tools for reading evidence about whole populations. They show patterns across large groups of people. For anything concerning your own health, speak to a doctor. Each tool lists its own sources.
foot_created: Created by Wenxin Wan — Lyon, France
exp_h1: Some exposures cause cancer. Some might. Telling them apart is the whole job.
exp_lede: Every mark behind this text is real: 185 exposures, 68 types of cancer, and the 466 links the World Health Organization's cancer agency has recorded between them.
exp_whatsin_h2: The exposures the IARC has linked to a cancer, graded by how certain the evidence is.
exp_bar1_note: Studies in people agree closely enough to rule out chance, bias and other explanations. This is the strongest conclusion the IARC draws.
exp_bar2_note: A causal reading of the association is credible, but chance, bias or confounding cannot yet be ruled out. The question remains open, and more research may settle it either way.
exp_reads_h2: Three limits of this map, worth knowing before you read it.
exp_read1_h3: Something that can cause cancer may still have had nothing to do with yours.
exp_read1_p: A Group 1 classification means an exposure can cause cancer under some conditions. How much, for how long, at what age, and which genes you carry all stand between that finding and any one person.
exp_read2_h3: A missing link may only mean nobody has looked hard enough yet.
exp_read2_p: The map records what has been studied and reviewed. Many gaps come from limited research funding or short follow-up time, so an empty space here is weak evidence of safety.
exp_read3_h3: This map describes populations, and cannot judge any single case.
exp_read3_p: If you are living with a cancer diagnosis, the people treating you know things about your case that no population map contains. Bring your questions to them.
exp_cta_h2: Start from a cancer. Start from an exposure. Or open the whole map.
exp_cta_lede: Free, in ten languages. Drag, zoom, and focus on any part of the network. Access is limited to reviewers while the scientific revision completes.
exp_cta_source: Source: IARC Monographs, "Classifications by cancer site", Volumes 1–141a (last update 18 May 2026), adapted from Schubauer-Berigan et al., JNCI Monographs 2026. This tool identifies hazards across whole populations. For anything concerning your own health, speak to a doctor.

meta_games_title: Sol & the UV Shield Quest — a sun-safety game — EpiDetective
meta_games_desc: A browser game for children aged 6 to 12 about smart sun habits: check the UV Index, find shade, cover up, and use sunscreen correctly. Free, no download, nothing collected.
games_sub: A side-scrolling adventure that teaches children how to enjoy the sun without harming their skin.
games_p1: Most skin cancers are caused by ultraviolet radiation, and the habits that prevent them are learned young. In this game Sol runs, jumps and collects sun stars across five regions, from a grassy meadow to a snowy mountain. Along the way Sol picks up a broad-brimmed hat and SPF 30+ sunscreen, loses the sunscreen after a swim, and reaches checkpoints where a quiz question must be answered before the path opens again.
games_p2: The questions cover what the UV Index means, when protection matters (UV 3 and above), why shade, clothing and sunscreen work best together, how sand, water and snow reflect UV, and why tanning beds should be avoided. Wrong answers are never punished: Sol is nudged back with a hint and a laugh. The game runs in your browser, works on a phone, and collects no data. It is in English.
games_fact_questions: questions in the bank, 5 per run
games_step1: Press Play. On a keyboard, move with A D or ← → and jump with Space. On a phone, use the on-screen buttons. A game controller works too.
games_step2: Collect sun coins and the nine hidden sun stars. Some platforms move, some fall, so keep moving.
games_step3: Watch the UV Index in the top bar. It changes from region to region, and drops when Sol stands in shade.
games_step4: At each checkpoint, read the question and jump up beneath one of the three answer blocks. The right answer opens the gate; a wrong one gives a hint and another try.
games_step5: Press <kbd>R</kbd> to restart. The cog opens the settings: voice narration, high contrast, a dyslexia-friendly font, larger text, game speed and touch-control size.
games_regions_h: The five regions and their UV Index
games_fine: The game uses an original character and artwork. Its source is open at github.com/Wenxin-Wan/sun-safety-adventure. The sun-safety advice follows the European Code Against Cancer and WHO guidance on UV protection.
